About

I study aerospace engineering at MIT, Course 16, focused on aerodynamics, computational fluid dynamics, and propulsion. Before MIT I earned an Associate of Interdisciplinary Science in Mechanical Engineering from South Texas College, back home in McAllen, Texas.

On MIT Motorsports I sit on the aerodynamics subteam, running CFD in STAR-CCM+ and ANSYS Fluent. But a race team doesn't let you stay in the software — the same wing you simulate is one you end up sanding a foam plug for, laying prepreg over, and bolting to the car. That loop from prediction to part to track is the part of engineering I care about.

I'm also joining MIT's Wright Brothers Wind Tunnel under Prof. Mark Drela, working on wall and blockage correction methods so tunnel data stays trustworthy — which closes the last side of that loop: simulation, manufacturing, and measurement.

I'm looking for internships in aerodynamics, CFD, and FEA, in commercial aerospace, motorsports, or space.

Selected work

Aerodynamic surfaces, composite structures, and the testing behind them — all built and tested in the MIT Motorsports shop.

01

Rear wing mounting retrofit

MIT Motorsports · aero · solo

The rear wing needed new mounting after the original arrangement no longer worked with the car as built. I took the retrofit on alone — working out how the wing would attach to the chassis, then designing and fabricating the spacers that set its height and angle.

A mount is not a bracket problem. Where the wing sits decides the angle of attack it actually runs at, and every millimetre of stack-up error shows up as downforce you predicted but did not get. The spacers are what make the installed geometry match the geometry the aero was designed around.

Mounting designSpacer fabricationInstalled geometry
02

Wing element manufacture — foam plug to prepreg

MIT Motorsports · composites

Every aero surface on the car starts as a foam plug shaped to the designed profile and sealed with epoxy, so resin cannot soak into the foam and so the cured part releases cleanly. Getting that surface right matters: whatever imperfection is on the plug ends up on the wing, and on an aero surface that is a real aerodynamic penalty, not a cosmetic one.

From there the elements are laid up in prepreg — carbon pre-impregnated with resin, which gives a far more consistent fibre-to-resin ratio than wet layup — then bagged and cured. The result is a stiff, light element that holds the section it was designed to hold under load.

Prepreg layupFoam plug prepVacuum baggingAero surfaces
03

Large composite bodywork panel

MIT Motorsports · composites

A large composite panel laid up over sealed foam moulds and vacuum bagged in two sections. Parts at this scale are their own problem — bag leaks, resin distribution, and keeping an even cure across a big surface all get harder the bigger the part gets.

Demoulding is the unglamorous half. The cured shell comes away with foam still bonded to the inside face, and all of it has to be dug out and the flanges trimmed back before the part can be fitted to the car.

Large-part layupVacuum baggingDemouldingTrimming
04

Composite layup characterization

MIT Motorsports · materials testing

Before committing a layup schedule to a structural part, we characterized the material. The team built a matrix of carbon coupons varying weave (plain vs. twill), ply count (3, 4, 5), orientation (0/90/0/90, 0/45/45/0, 0/90/90/0), and cure schedule, logging initial and final carbon-to-resin ratio for each — final ratios ran from roughly 50:50 up to 83:17 depending on layup and cure.

Coupons were then pulled in tension and compression on an Instron. Those force-displacement curves are what decided which schedule was actually worth cutting parts from, instead of picking a layup off a datasheet and hoping.

Coupon testingInstronTension & compressionLayup selection
05

Impact attenuator crush testing

MIT Motorsports · structures

FSAE requires the car to carry an impact attenuator that absorbs a specified amount of energy without exceeding a deceleration limit. That has to be proven by test, not asserted.

Candidate structures were run to failure on the Instron — a thin-wall metal tube and an aluminium honeycomb block bonded to an anti-intrusion plate. Area under the force-displacement curve gives energy absorbed; the peak of the curve sets the deceleration a driver would actually take. Afterwards the crush pattern reads straight off the honeycomb cells.

Energy absorptionCrush testingRules compliance
06

Carbon fiber driver seat

MIT Motorsports · composites

A one-off seat shell laid up over a foam plug sanded to the driver-fit profile and sealed with epoxy. The seat is a packaging part as much as a structural one — it has to hold the driver in the position the cockpit was designed around and survive being sat in, hard, for an entire event.

Like every plug-moulded part, it comes off the mould with foam bonded to the inside face, which is cleared out by hand before the flange is trimmed back.

Wet layupMould prepDemoulding & finishing
07

Composite battery enclosure

MIT Motorsports · EV packaging

The accumulator container for the car's battery pack — a bonded carbon composite box with aluminium edge reinforcement, divided internally into segments with copper foil routing between compartments.

It is a packaging problem as much as a structural one. The box has to hold the pack, survive its load case, satisfy the rules on enclosure and electrical isolation, and still fit the volume the chassis leaves for it.

Bonded assemblyComposite panelsEV packaging
